papers.title: The Language that Gets People to Give: Phrases that Predict Success on Kickstarter
papers.study_kind: observational predictive modeling with post-hoc qualitative interpretation
papers.scope: Kickstarter public crowdfunding pitches and rewards, 13 creative categories; pages scraped August 2012 after campaign end; funding outcome is goal achieved, not proposal merit or fulfillment.
papers.sample_and_design: 45,815 launched-project URLs, 45,810 retained after five non-ended; lasso logistic regression of 20,391 selected 1–3 grams plus 59 controls, ten-fold cross-validation and 80/20 train/test comparison. Homepages can change while campaign is live and include reward descriptions; controls include update counts, comments and Featured/Most Funded placement measured post hoc.
papers.outcomes: Binary funded versus not funded. No randomized wording intervention, reader understanding, funder decision mechanism or subsequent delivery outcome.

findings.interpretation_limits: US Kickstarter projects observed in 2012; not all proposal settings.

findings.claim: Reported cross-validation error was 17.03% controls-only versus 2.4% with phrases and controls (Table 2); Figure 3 reports 2.41% cross-validation and 2.24% held-out prediction error for alpha=1 using an 80/20 split.
findings.denominator: 45,810 campaign observations, ten-fold CV; split details not fully specified
findings.interpretation_limits: Retrospective homepage text and dynamic controls can include outcome information; neither evaluation establishes prospective launch-time performance. Figure 4 and adjacent prose do not clearly identify the metric basis.

findings.claim: Paper calls 58.56% a deviance drop/variance: given reported null, control and combined deviances 63,463.47, 37,525.52 and 363.42, the increment 37,162.10 divided by null deviance is 58.56%; relative to controls-only deviance it is about 99.03%.
findings.interpretation_limits: Not ordinary variance explained or a causal contribution; deviance from fitted models and wording internally inconsistent.

findings.claim: Positive and negative sentiment differences were reported statistically nonsignificant; the paper calls LIWC group differences small despite statistical significance.
findings.denominator: funded and unfunded campaign language groups; sample-level sentiment test denominator not separately stated
findings.interpretation_limits: Do not infer that positivity improves funding or no real effect exists.

limitations: Homepages were scraped after end and could have changed; page 10 shows live progress ("we’ve hit the 50% mark"). Updates, comments and Most Funded status are dynamic. Strong potential temporal leakage and reverse causation, not resolved by cross-validation.
No random assignment, no inference about individual phrases causing funding; category-wide filtering and Google presence do not establish transfer.

Paper describes the majority-class baseline as always choosing not-funded despite funded being the majority; 48.47% baseline error corresponds to predicting funded (pages 3 and 6). Figure 4 and adjacent prose do not clearly identify the metric basis; Figure 3 distinguishes cross-validation from held-out prediction error.
No independent prelaunch validation, calibration or selection-inside-fold audit established in supplied paper.
rule_implications: No lexical positive/negative phrase scoring, automatic assertiveness increase or funding guarantee. Clear, factual rewards and audience benefits may be worth presenting when true and relevant; reciprocity interpretation is an untested mechanism.
Reaffirm skills/write-with-purpose/references/concepts-and-claims.md: separate proposals, evidence, predictions and actual outcomes; preserve uncertainty.
data_or_code_leads: Paper page 11 lists historical KS.predicts and Gg.KS.pos/neg author URLs; access, version, data and rights not checked in this review. glmnet software is identified but no project code verified. No automatic GitHub adoption.
extraction_issues: Page 5 says 58.56% drop without clearly stating denominator; direct calculation shown above. Figure 3 distinguishes 2.41% cross-validation error from 2.24% held-out prediction error at alpha=1; Table 2 rounds cross-validation error to 2.4%. Figure 4 and adjacent prose are metric-ambiguous.

papers.title: Use of Promotional Language in Grant Applications and Grant Success
papers.study_kind: cross-sectional observational association study with regression and lexical validation
papers.scope: Biomedical grant applications to NNF in 2015–2022 and Northwestern faculty NIH submissions in 2007–2019; funded and rejected full application texts. Audience includes agency reviewers, not general workplace decision makers.
papers.sample_and_design: 9,096 NNF applications, 2,439 NIH applications from one university; dictionary fraction of 139 science-specific promotional words, logistic association with covariates including applicant performance and grant features and year/length fixed effects. Lexicon validation and five-fold cross-validation reported; released supplementary information and data statements not individually checked.
papers.outcomes: Binary funded/rejected and frequency of promotional terms; no randomized causal outcome, measured readability, merit or actual reviewer comprehension.

findings.claim: NNF awarded 1,579 of 9,096 applications (17.4%); NIH awarded 481 of 2,439 (19.7%).
findings.interpretation_limits: NIH cohort from one institution, NNF from one foundation; repeated applicants possible.

findings.claim: Adjusted odds ratios for promotional-word percentage were 1.47 (95% CI 1.25–1.71) NNF and 1.51 (1.10–2.11) NIH; methods indicate a one percentage-point increase in the fraction.
findings.denominator: 9,096 NNF and 2,439 NIH applications in full samples; exact model complete cases not stated in main text
findings.interpretation_limits: Odds ratios, not probability ratios or effects of editing. Figure 2 displays 1.46 for the NNF multivariable model; use prose 1.47 with rounding discrepancy flagged.

findings.claim: Mean dictionary-word fractions funded vs unfunded were 1.02% vs 0.98% for NNF and 0.93% vs 0.89% for NIH.
findings.interpretation_limits: Word fractions, not measures of inaccurate or unsupported hype; differences are descriptive.

findings.claim: NNF binscatter estimated 14% to 22% funding probability from lowest to highest promotional-language bin; paper also describes relative increase of 53%.
findings.denominator: 20 equal-size bins of NNF sample; exact bin counts not printed
findings.interpretation_limits: Approximate fitted sample association, not benefit from adding words; figure caption also calls 53% an odds increase, creating ambiguity.

findings.claim: Previous lexicon construction evaluated each candidate in at least 500 occurrences by two reviewers, with reported kappa 0.82.
findings.denominator: at least 500 contexts per candidate term, 139-term instrument
findings.interpretation_limits: Context-level agreement from earlier work; does not validate each token occurrence in every grant.

limitations: Observational covariate adjustment does not remove unmeasured project merit, reviewer expectations, selection or confounding; author notes need for causal studies (p8).
A dictionary term is not a judgment of exaggeration, truth or appropriateness in context. Their sample substitution examples are sometimes awkward or change intensity.
Five-fold validation reported (Fig 2) without predictive accuracy or independent temporal/external sample evaluation in main paper; does not establish causal or prospective performance.

Page 2 says 38.4% of NNF and 33.7% of NIH are women, with numerators using all applications although phrasing ambiguously follows awarded subset. Treat 3491/9096 and 823/2439 as full-application counts.
NIH sample and one private foundation do not represent other funders, disciplines or eras.
rule_implications: A blanket ban on adjectives or promotional lexemes conflicts with observed positive association, not proof of improved prose or reason to add adjectives.

Reaffirm evidence-backed positive emphasis and proposal significance when substantiated; retain uncertainty and voice. Flag ungrounded novelty, superlatives and promises for contextual review, never automatic deletion or insertion.
data_or_code_leads: Main paper pages 2, 9–10: NNF data obtainable through cooperative agreement on request; NIH data internal university request; supplement 1 lists dictionary, operationalization, model tables, supplement 2 data statement. Neither supplement inspected; no reproducible repository verified.
extraction_issues: Article uses causal wording ("can increase") but discussion explicitly calls for causal analyses; this review treats estimates as associations. NNF adjusted OR in main results 1.47 while figure 2 shows 1.46. Caption and text disagree about odds versus probability for 53% change.

papers.title: The effect of writing style on success in grant applications
papers.study_kind: observational multivariable study of application language and review outcomes
papers.scope: One early-career funding scheme in 2014, disciplinary panels; project description, abstract and CV; funding selection has staged review, later presentation and peer review.
papers.sample_and_design: 3,207 applications received; 3,030 consented, 2,900 text-extractable after exclusions, 2,532 eligible following field and bibliometric exclusions; tables use 2,493 first-stage and 677 second-stage descriptions. English proficiency proxied by country-level score. LIWC 2015 English dictionaries; features standardized by panel; mixed, ordinal and logistic regressions control for panel, applicant publication impact and gender.
papers.outcomes: First and second-stage project scores, ordinal final score and decision to proceed/funding. Linguistic proxies are not observed comprehension or objective writing quality.

findings.claim: First-stage project-description model estimated certainty coefficient B=0.043 (95% CI 0.022–0.063; p<0.001); tentative words B=0.002 (95% CI −0.020–0.023; p=0.885).
findings.evidence_locator: Table 3, mixed model with panel fixed effects
findings.interpretation_limits: Coefficients panel-standardized, observational, no causal proof; a null result does not justify removing hedges.

findings.claim: First-stage progression model certainty OR 1.180 (95% CI 1.070–1.303); tentative OR 0.986 (0.890–1.093). Causal words OR 1.050 (0.952–1.158), not statistically significant.
findings.interpretation_limits: Per standardized predictor under model covariates; not final grant success. Do not add unsupported certainty or causal wording.

findings.claim: First-stage project score associations include positive word count B=0.501 and squared term B=−0.360, and positive words/sentence B=0.135 with squared B=−0.159.
findings.interpretation_limits: Joint quadratic model, panel-standardized; do not turn into a target or claim that increasing length causes success.

findings.claim: In stage two, project score model common words B=−0.030, p=0.036; final funding model common words OR=0.863, 95% CI 0.707–1.053, p=0.146.
findings.interpretation_limits: Different outcomes; later-stage sample selected on earlier success. Paper overgeneralizes significance to both outcomes.

findings.claim: For final ordinal score model, Nagelkerke pseudo-R² was 0.191 for full model and 0.146 linguistic-only; first-stage progression 0.131 and 0.100 respectively.
findings.interpretation_limits: Pseudo-R² is model fit statistic, not ordinary variance explained or out-of-sample accuracy; no external model validation is reported.

findings.claim: Abstract model shows tentative words B=0.024, p=0.025 for stage-one project score; most other abstract associations were not statistically significant.
findings.interpretation_limits: Paper’s blanket conclusion of no abstract effects overstates its own table; exploratory multiple comparisons and proxy interpretation cautions.

limitations: Single year, one scheme, early career and pre-set section/page constraints. Excluded humanities, law and qualitative social sciences and applicants missing bibliometric records.

Country nationality-based English score is crude; LIWC common-word frequency conflates technical content with readability; LIWC analytic score is not demonstrated narrative quality; measures do not establish mechanisms.
Selection into second stage, intervening extended applications and oral panel presentation confound comparisons across stages.
No held-out prospective predictive assessment or causal intervention reported; significance is not measured effect of an edit.
Table 9 duplicates first-stage decision coefficients in last column, and Table 3 extracted confidence intervals have apparent inconsistencies; verify typeset table before reuse.
rule_implications: Refine plain-language suggestions to preserve necessary technical content and vary syntax for reader function; do not impose short sentences, simple words or a complexity target.
Reaffirm preserving uncertainty; tentative terms not shown harmful, and may be epistemically necessary; candidate reassurance cannot raise modality.
Use section and audience context when reviewing presentation rather than translating LIWC narrative and analytic indexes into paragraph-function labels.
data_or_code_leads: LIWC 2015 identified as third-party software, not a demonstrated open corpus or codebook; applications collected under consent and no reusable release verified.
extraction_issues: Paper uses effect/causal language despite observational design. Narrative interpretations are proxies; Table 10 conflicts with blanket abstract null conclusion, Table 7 with blanket stage-two common-words statement.

cross_paper_synthesis: All three studies are observational; award success or statistical prediction is not comprehension, scientific quality or a causal effect of rewriting. P03 retrospective end-state predictors raise strong temporal leakage concerns.

Promotional vocabulary has positive adjusted funding associations in P10, while P11 shows nonlinear and section-dependent linguistic associations plus non-significant tentative-word estimates. These results contradict blanket adjective removal and qualify blanket simplicity guidance, but do not support adding hype, certainty or complexity.
P03 concerns rewards-based crowdfunding; P10 biomedical funders; P11 one early-career funding round and panels. They are different samples, not independent replications of one mechanism.

Existing preserve-voice, source-fidelity and uncertainty guidance already captures the strongest supported editorial principle; an author-controlled claim-to-evidence and context check is a plausible advantage to test, not a measured advantage.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/SKILL.md: organize around reader question and select evidence; references/concepts-and-claims.md: distinguish proposal from evidence
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Author requests a proposal or decision memo and its purpose, audience and source material are available.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Track supplied claim-to-source links and unfilled claim-evidence slots, labeled unresolved when extraction is uncertain.
proposed_rule_changes.judgment: Assess whether rationale, material benefits, costs, risks and actionable request are supported and relevant; preserve truthful positive emphasis and author choice.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Make merit and consequences legible without generic promotional phrases.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A speculative concept may validly state a hoped-for benefit if explicitly marked as a hypothesis; no mandate to supply absent facts.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/references/language-and-meaning.md: preserve uncertainty and force; edit-with-purpose/SKILL.md: preserve source context
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: A proposed edit strengthens novelty, confidence, causal direction, certainty, comparative claims or commitments.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Highlight changed modal, negation, number, comparative and superlative tokens as review candidates; do not decide entailment by token matching.
proposed_rule_changes.judgment: Compare full claim, context and underlying source, retain warranted qualifiers; allow genuinely supported assertive wording and accurate adjectives.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Support persuasive emphasis without making claims stronger than their evidence.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: Replacing an unnecessarily tentative assertion with a stronger one can be valid if the supplied source actually supports it.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/SKILL.md: keep technical terms and avoid uniform sentence-length preference
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: A sentence is difficult for the intended reader or hides a relevant relation in a proposal or memo.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Flag only declared word limits and optionally show observed word/sentence counts without a target.
proposed_rule_changes.judgment: Compare alternatives for recoverable meaning, technical precision, audience needs and rhythm; preserve complexity necessary for the argument.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Improve explanation while retaining technical substance and voice.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A specialist evaluator may need a precise technical term and a multi-clause qualification.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: docs/writing-harness/accepted-foundations.md: Family → Form → Section; features are observations, not targets
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Reviewing decision-oriented forms with author-supplied purpose and evidence.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Show optional checklist slots for decision, options and support only when explicitly requested or required.
proposed_rule_changes.judgment: Check whether proposed action, alternatives and consequences are understandable for this decision; do not require fixed sequence or all slots.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Possible form-sensitive support and comparison, not demonstrated funding advantage.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A short memo may legitimately address one narrow decision with alternatives linked separately.

github_reuse: No GitHub repository was established by these three papers. P03 historical author-hosted coefficient files, P10 supplementary lexicon and access-controlled application data, and LIWC are leads requiring separate access and rights checks. Do not equate imported lexical cues, section labels, relation annotations or paragraph functions.
Dataset adoption notes recommend source version, original labels, span boundaries and rights, and keep structural roles and passage functions separate; no imported tool installed or evaluated.
Local function calibration 21/36 versus 18/36 exact-set agreement is no validation of new rhetorical function classifications; apply no function quotas and do not infer function-length profiles.
open_questions: Were P03 dynamic text and features available at the time a prediction would actually be made, and was all feature selection inside each training fold?
Can P10 supplements resolve complete-case sample counts and per-percentage-point model units, and disclose data rights and uncertainty for cross-validation?
Can P11 typeset tables resolve duplicated CV column and confidence-interval discrepancies, and would section-specific patterns hold in another funding program?
Would human raters and authors judge evidence-linked emphasis more accurate, useful and voice-faithful than blanket anti-hype edits, without optimizing funding?
